extracted.intended_audience: current and prospective peer reviewers for The BMJ (clinician and patient reviewers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for clinicians and patient reviewers who are asked to peer review manuscripts for The BMJ, covering expectations about openness, priorities, procedures, and ethical checks. Focuses on what reviewers should do and how their reports may be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sign reports and declare competing interests
rubrics_metrics.description: We ask reviewers to sign their reports and declare any competing interests on any manuscripts we send them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The BMJ operates open peer review: reviewers are asked to sign reports and those signed comments will be part of the prepublication history posted alongside accepted research and analysis articles (accepted research papers submitted from September 2014 onwards; analysis articles from February 2016 onwards). If you experience any adverse event arising from open peer review or wish to comment on it, email the BMJ. Declare competing interests whenever reviewing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise manuscripts by originality, importance, and reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Help us prioritise manuscripts, bearing in mind that The BMJ aims to publish original, important, and reliable articles that will help our readers around the world to make better decisions about practice, policy, education, and research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing suitability, consider whether the work is original, important, and reliable and whether it will be useful to The BMJ’s mainly clinical readership. All research in The BMJ is published open access, which may affect relevance. Use these priorities when recommending triage, revise, or reject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide constructive critique to help editors assess importance and originality
rubrics_metrics.description: For the best reviews (those that constructively critique the article and help editors assess its importance and originality) we offer, in partnership with Cleveland Clinic Foundation, up to 3 AMA PRA Category 1 CME points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write reviews that are constructive and focused on helping editors judge importance and originality. Reviewers advise editors, who make the final decision (sometimes aided by an editorial manuscript committee). Manuscripts are usually seen by at least two reviewers and reviewers can access each other's reports once The BMJ has made its decision; constructive, professional tone is therefore important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check study protocol and methodological/reporting rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: The prepublication history comprises all previous versions of the manuscript, the study protocol for research papers (submitting the protocol is mandatory for all clinical trials and encouraged for all other studies at The BMJ), the report from the manuscript committee meeting, the reviewers’ signed comments, and the authors’ responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a reviewer, examine the submitted protocol (mandatory for trials) and compare it to the manuscript to assess adherence, completeness, and transparency. Assess methodological rigor and reporting quality; note that protocol and prior versions will be posted with accepted articles, so checks you make may be visible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and report ethical issues, plagiarism, duplicate publication, or scientific fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: The BMJ transparency policy pulls together many separate editorial policies; it includes advice on what to do if you are concerned about the ethics aspects of a manuscript or if you suspect plagiarism, duplicate publication, or scientific fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you have ethical concerns, suspected plagiarism, duplicate publication, or fraud, follow the instructions in The BMJ transparency policy and raise these concerns with the editors. The transparency policy provides procedures and contact points for such issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond promptly to review invitations and manage conflicts
rubrics_metrics.description: If we need your help with appraising a manuscript we will email you and ask you to accept or reject the reviewing invitation at our online editorial office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept or decline invitations promptly via the online editorial office so editors can allocate reviewers efficiently. When accepting, ensure you can meet deadlines and that you declare any competing interests as required. Reviewers typically form part of a panel of at least two reviewers for a manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider patient perspective on importance and relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to peer review, we also ask patient reviewers for their opinion on the importance and relevance of selected manuscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When relevant, give thought to the likely importance and relevance of the work for patients and the public. The BMJ is committed to partnerships between doctors and patients, and patient-review contributions help judge practical relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare reviews knowing they may be published and transferred within BMJ
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors can nominate other BMJ Journals for automatic transfer if rejected, and the system passes on editors' comments and peer reviewers' reports relating to that manuscript; a review provided for The BMJ may be seen later by other editors within BMJ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that reviews and editorial comments may be shared internally between BMJ journals and, for accepted items, reviewers' signed comments and the manuscript's prepublication history may be posted online. Maintain appropriate professional tone and confidentiality consistent with this possibility.
